narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 91% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the law school sets a high bar for admission, this strong prediction of failure led directly to the rejection of your application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your first-year and third-year class rankings were by far the most influential. Both placed you in the bottom decile of your school—far below the average of around the 6th decile for students who were accepted. These unusually low rankings strongly pushed the model toward expecting you to struggle with the bar exam. Your undergraduate GPA was the third most important factor; at 3.10 it was modestly below the 3.23 average of admitted students and therefore also nudged the prediction slightly toward failure.

Taken together, these academic signals outweighed other details such as your middle-income background, your plan to attend full-time, and your LSAT score of 30.

To improve your chances, you should focus on strengthening your academic performance and consider retaking the LSAT to raise your score. Many students successfully reapply after showing clear improvement in these areas. (198 words)
